Google Right to Be Forgotten Form: A Step-by-Step Guide for Italy

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

The Google right to be forgotten form is an online request under EU data protection law that asks Google to stop showing specific URLs when people search for your name. It works best when you prepare the evidence first, describe each link separately and explain why the information is inaccurate, outdated or no longer relevant to the public. Below is the procedure we follow for clients in Italy, field by field.

What the form can and cannot achieve

A successful request removes selected links from Google results for searches on your name; it does not delete the page itself. The page stays online and can still be reached through other queries. This delisting mechanism comes from the Google Spain ruling of the EU Court of Justice (C-131/12) and is now anchored in Article 17 GDPR, the right to erasure, read together with the Italian Codice Privacy.

Because the legal test is a balance between your privacy and the public's interest in finding the information, Google evaluates every URL on its own merits. A request is not a complaint about the website, and it is not the right channel for copyright problems, impersonation or explicit images, which have dedicated Google procedures. If you are still unsure whether your case qualifies at all, our analysis of what the right to be forgotten can really remove from Google covers the substantive limits; this guide focuses on the practical filing.

What to prepare before you start

Gather all material before opening the form, because the session can expire and an incomplete submission usually comes back with a request for more information.

  • The exact URLs. Copy each address from the results page, not from the homepage of the site. Include every version that appears: mobile pages, AMP copies, syndicated reprints and image results.
  • The search terms. Note the queries that trigger the links, usually your full name, sometimes name plus city (for example "Mario Rossi Milano") or name plus profession.
  • Proof of identity. A scan of an identity document. Google allows you to obscure parts that are not needed to confirm who you are, such as the photo or document number, as long as the name remains legible.
  • Supporting documents. An acquittal or dismissal decision, a court annotation under the Riforma Cartabia (art. 64-ter disp. att. c.p.p.), a certificate showing a company was closed, or a letter proving that a role ended years ago.
  • A power of attorney if a lawyer or agency files on your behalf, stating that they are authorised to act for you in data protection matters.

How to fill in each field of the request

Start by selecting Italy as the country whose law applies, because this determines which legal framework and which reviewing team handle the case. The Google right to be forgotten form sits in the Legal Help centre under the request to remove personal information under European privacy law.

Identity and representation

Enter the name you use in searches exactly as it appears in the results, including middle names or maiden names if those trigger the links. If someone else is filing, the form asks for the representative's name and their relationship to you; this is where the power of attorney becomes relevant.

URLs and explanations

For each URL you will find a separate box asking how the page relates to you and why it should be delisted. Treat these boxes as small legal arguments. Write two or three precise paragraphs per link rather than one generic text pasted everywhere: Google's reviewers compare your explanation with the actual page, and copy-paste justifications are a frequent reason for refusal.

Declaration and signature

The final section requires you to confirm that the information is accurate and to type your name as a signature, with the date.

How to argue a right to be forgotten request convincingly

A persuasive right to be forgotten request explains, link by link, why your interest in privacy now outweighs the public interest in accessing the information through your name.

The strongest elements are usually these: the passage of time since the events, the fact that you are a private person rather than a public figure, the inaccuracy or incompleteness of the content, a later judicial outcome that the article does not mention, and the concrete harm the result causes today, for example in job applications or banking relationships. Sensitive categories of data, such as health information or criminal allegations that never led to a conviction, deserve particular emphasis because the GDPR protects them more strongly.

Reviewers decide on facts, not feelings: one dated document proving that the story ended differently is worth more than a page describing how distressing the result is.

Avoid attacking the journalist or the website, and do not claim the content is defamatory unless you have a court decision saying so. Defamation under art. 595 c.p. is for Italian courts; delisting is a privacy balancing exercise.

Timelines and what happens after you submit

Once you click submit, Google sends an automatic confirmation with a reference number, and a decision normally follows within several weeks, although complex cases can take longer. Article 12 GDPR sets a one-month response deadline that can be extended by two further months when requests are complex or numerous.

  1. Confirmation email with the case reference, which you should keep for every later step.
  2. Possible request for clarification, typically asking for a missing document or a clearer link between you and a page. Reply in the same email thread.
  3. Decision per URL. Google may accept some links and reject others in the same case, with a short explanation for each refusal.
  4. Implementation. Accepted URLs disappear from name searches on Google across EU and EEA countries, and Google uses location signals to limit access from Europe to other versions.

Google may inform the webmaster that a page has been delisted, without disclosing your identity.

Common mistakes that lead to refusal in Italy

Most refusals we see in Italy stem from preparation errors rather than from weak cases. Submitting a newspaper homepage instead of the article URL, omitting the search query or forgetting syndicated copies are all avoidable.

A second group of errors concerns the argument itself. Asking to delist recent news about an ongoing investigation, a current public office or an active business role rarely succeeds, because the public interest is still strong; it is wiser to wait until the facts have aged or the proceedings have ended.

Finally, some people expect the form to clean up every negative result. When a page cannot be delisted, other routes such as an update request to the publisher or building stronger positive results may be more realistic; the differences between these approaches are explained in our article on removal, deindexing and ranking suppression.

When to involve a specialist

Filing on your own is perfectly possible for one or two clear links, while professional support pays off when the case involves criminal proceedings, many URLs or a previous refusal. In those situations the drafting of each explanation, the choice of supporting documents and the sequence of requests make a real difference.

If Google rejects the request, you can ask it to reconsider with new evidence, file a complaint (reclamo) with the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali, or go to an Italian civil court. Knowing how to request Google right to be forgotten delisting properly the first time keeps those options stronger, because the original submission becomes part of the record.
